title: Independent judicial interpretation after Loper Bright
shortTitle: Independent judicial interpretation after Loper Bright
summary: Independent judgment requires the reviewing court to determine a statute’s meaning with its own legal analysis while considering useful agency expertise and honoring actual delegations.
notes:
A reviewing court first asks whether the challenged action falls within the statute’s authority. Under Loper Bright’s reading of APA § 706, the court uses traditional interpretive tools to reach the best statutory reading. It may draw on an agency’s informed interpretation, but statutory ambiguity alone does not transfer the choice of meaning to the agency. The majority treats this as the legal task Congress assigned to reviewing courts. (Printed 943–949, 953.)

The court must separately identify discretion that the statute actually confers. An express instruction for the agency to define a term, an authorization to fill details, or language allowing a reasonable or appropriate policy choice can grant real decisionmaking room. The court identifies its extent and tests whether the agency exercised it through reasoned decisionmaking. This preserves the separate operation of State Farm review over policy choices within the statutory boundaries. (Printed 945–946, 950, 963–964.)

The opinions disagree about both history and institutional capacity. Kagan maintains that some ambiguities leave policy choices that agencies are better equipped and more accountable to make, and that § 706 does not command de novo review. The majority responds that expertise can inform a court and that legal interpretation remains judicial even in technical disputes. The majority’s statutory holding leaves constitutional questions about legislatively specified standards of review for further analysis; Thomas’s concurrence would impose a constitutional restriction as well. (Printed 949–960, 961–963.)
